title: Shemira: Answering Cain's Question
hook: after death the body is watched over until burial
carry: the dead are honored, never left alone

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was vidui, and your line was ready. This week walked from communities that differ, to peace at home, to endings, beginnings, and the bedside. Today it ends past the last breath.

Two in the morning. A quiet room at a funeral home, one lamp on. In the next room, under a sheet, lies a woman who died yesterday afternoon. In this room, in a plain chair, sits someone with a book of Psalms open on their knee. Maybe a grandson. Maybe a stranger from the synagogue who signed up for the night shift. They read a little, they sit, they keep awake. At six, someone else will take the chair. Between death and burial, she will not be left by herself for a minute.
screen: `TWO IN THE MORNING.` → `A CHAIR AND A BOOK OF PSALMS.` → `SHE IS NOT LEFT ALONE.`

segments.voice: Shomer means a guard, a keeper, a watcher, and you met it in your very first year, in Cain's mouth. After Abel is killed, God asks Cain where his brother is, and Cain answers, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "am I my brother's keeper?" Keeper there is shomer. Cain meant no. The one in the chair at two in the morning is answering yes. The practice is called shemira, watching. Why watch someone who has died? The body once held a person made in the image of God, and Jewish law treats it with honor: kavod ha-met, honor for the dead. It isn't set aside like an object while the paperwork gets done. Some also teach that the soul lingers near the body until burial, and the watcher keeps it company. Tradition says to read Psalms, or simply to sit in quiet, and not to eat or chat in the room. The Talmud even exempts someone watching the dead from certain other commandments, because they are busy with this one. Family watch, if they can. When they can't, volunteers from the community step in, sometimes in shifts through the night, often for someone they never met. So this week ends where it began, with communities: different practices, different homes, and in the end, a chair by the door, and someone in it.

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who has died, not their last day but an ordinary one: their voice in the kitchen, a joke they told too often. Keep them company for a few breaths, the way a shomer would, and if you pray, read a psalm for them or sit in silence. If a loss ever feels too heavy to carry alone, please reach out: in the US, call or text 988, any hour; elsewhere, local emergency help.
Shomer. The keeper who sits with the body from death to burial, reading Psalms or keeping quiet, answering Cain's question with yes. Today's word.

howItsDone: In Jewish communities that keep this custom, family members or volunteers take turns sitting with the body from death until the funeral, a practice called shemira; the shomer often reads Psalms.
